column2: Below him was a smooth chute spiraling downward. He had never experienced such an extravagant waterslide; for thrills and excitement, it easily surpassed the log flume at a water park.
The only problem was that smiling attendants greeted you at the bottom of the log flume. God knew what waited down here. Perhaps a dragon’s mouth, ready for a midnight snack.
“Ow!”

He landed on his backside—or, more precisely, on something. It was a smooth landing, almost carefree and pleasant. They continued descending afterward, but the log flume had given way to a Ferris wheel. They looked at each other, then down beneath their feet.

They were sitting side by side on a gigantic waterwheel. The bronze wheel was wrapped in a thick layer of unknown fabric, and each paddle that caught the water was a comfortable seat. They descended through a dark passage, the sound of rushing water on both sides.
At last light appeared ahead, and Lu Mingfei and Nono jumped off together.
“Does this count as… trespassing in someone’s home?” Lu Mingfei looked around, unable to believe his eyes.

He had expected a vast, magnificent palace, with ancient Greek columns or great pillars carved with coiling dragons in the old Chinese style. Above them would be an immense dome, surely with bronze dragon heads in its decorated ceiling; a high platform with a throne on it; and statues of snake-faced men standing on every side. Add flowing mercury on the floor, mountains and rivers cast in bronze, and eternal lamps fueled by dozens of vats of mermaid oil, and the place would have been even more fitting for a Dragon King.
But now they stood in a little house, an ancient dwelling cast in bronze. Apart from its material, it was no different from the old Chinese homes he had seen in history-book illustrations.
It even had windows, though outside them stood a black metal wall.
A small bronze lamp gave the room its light. It was shaped like a palace maid kneeling on a table, holding the lamp in one hand and curving the sleeve of the other over the shade.
“The Changxin Palace Lamp!” Lu Mingfei had learned about it in history class. One had been unearthed from the tomb of Liu Sheng, Prince Jing of Zhongshan.

“It’s a Han-dynasty lamp. Perfect design: oil enters from below, and smoke goes out through the sleeve.” Nono walked around it, studying it. “But this design is far more advanced than the Changxin Palace Lamp. It must have a very large oil reservoir and a mechanism pumping oil from it to here. Even after more than a thousand years, it hasn’t run dry.”
“This is the Dragon King’s bedchamber?” Lu Mingfei muttered. “Comrade Dragon King lived a simple life, and he doesn’t look very big, either.”
He relaxed. There was nothing strange here, no dragons and no big eggs. It was rather cozy, in fact.

“The communications cable was cut on the way down.” Nono touched the half-length of black cable still attached to her belt. “It’s all right, though. We’ll use your blood to open the entrance again in a moment. Once we’re outside, we can reconnect the cable.”
“Ah!” Lu Mingfei remembered and quickly put his finger in his mouth.

“Does it hurt that much?” Nono glanced at him. “I only borrowed a tiny bit of blood. Still, it was a good thing I brought you. You’re a better blood sample than the Key, and you can even swim on your own.”
“It’s not the pain. I’m disinfecting it!” Lu Mingfei mumbled around his finger. “So many dead people rotted in that water. Who knows how many germs are in it? Saliva disinfects.”

“They’ve been dead for thousands of years, and this place is sealed. There’s nothing alive here. Even if there were germs before, they’d have died long ago,” Nono said. “Besides, you know dead bodies soaked in that water, and you still put your finger in your mouth?”
Lu Mingfei’s stomach churned. He belched several times, hurriedly took out his finger, and spat repeatedly, yet his mouth still seemed to have a strange taste.

Ignoring him, Nono ran her hand along the bronze wall and walked slowly farther in. The place lay below the water and was so well sealed that, after more than a thousand years, it held not a speck of dust. The furnishings were remarkably spare. Two of the three rooms were bedrooms, with rattan beds still sturdy after all this time. The scrolls on the wall had not been so fortunate: Lu Mingfei brushed one with his finger, and the silk crumbled, leaving a bare wooden roller to fall and roll away. A ceramic vase stood on a low table, holding a thoroughly withered flower whose black stem looked like drawn wire. Two white robes hung on the wall, looking at first glance like a tall and a short person standing against it. In the main room, a stack of yellowed coarse paper lay on a low table. The writing, in neat Han clerical script, was still legible. Lu Mingfei glanced at an incomplete sentence: “Twelfth year of Longxing, divination, unclear…”
The room gave him a strange feeling, as though thousands of years had frozen here and the scent of those who once lived in it still lingered.
Nono was unusually quiet, paying close attention to everything. Lu Mingfei did not dare disturb her. He followed her through the rooms and finally sat close beside her at the little table.
“Sit opposite me,” Nono said.
“Oh.” Lu Mingfei had no choice but to move to the other side.
He watched her. Her gaze was unfocused and distant.
“It’s all right. Don’t talk. I’m thinking.” Nono waved a hand at him, her gaze still distant.

Besides the stack of coarse paper, the little table held delicate porcelain cups, a pot, and bowls. Slowly Nono reached out, picked up the pot with one hand and a small cup with the other, and mimed pouring water. The pot was empty and nothing came out, yet she did it so convincingly, watching the rim of the cup, that one could almost imagine she really saw it gradually fill. Then she set the cup before Lu Mingfei and spoke in the gentle voice of an older sister. “Are you thirsty? Have some water.”
“Senior, don’t scare me… If you’re going to go crazy, at least wait until we get back!” Lu Mingfei was alarmed.
“You’re the one who’s crazy. Your whole family is crazy!” Nono glared at him. “I told you not to talk!”
“Oh.” Lu Mingfei breathed easier. He did not know what she was doing, but her fierce tone gave him back a little of the familiar Nono.
“Why aren’t you speaking?” Her gaze went distant again.

Lu Mingfei wanted to say: Senior, if you want to put on a play, wait until we get back. Then I’ll play whatever you want with you. If you’re Mu Guiying, I’ll be Yang Zongbao. If you’re Tang Sanzang, I’ll be Sun Wukong. If you’re Zhu Bajie stealing watermelons, I’ll play the village watchman. But right now we ought to throw down the bomb and leave!
“I’m a little tired.” Yet, as if caught by Nono’s strange mood, the words slipped out of him like those of someone just home.

He thought of the two white robes on the wall and suddenly understood what she was doing. Two people, not one, had once lived in this house. Nono was reenacting a conversation they might have had here.
The Dragon King Norton was two people! No wonder, after he had dealt with that dragon at the college, he had been given this secret mission: there was another Norton!
Could the two Dragon Kings called Norton really have sat facing each other and talking like this in this humble “bedchamber” so many years ago?
Two bedrooms, two white robes, two people. One sat with a stack of paper before him, writing; the other poured him water and watched him.

Nono gently stroked the edge of the little table. A clicking sound came from inside the wall, which opened to let a bronze puppet slide out along a track and kneel beside the table. On the tray in its hands were grapes so shriveled they were almost unrecognizable.
“That’s high-tech! This Dragon King was a real tech geek!” Lu Mingfei stared.
Nono delicately picked something from the bronze tray and held out to him an imaginary bunch of fresh, green grapes.
With the play having reached this point, he could hardly refuse to go on. Lu Mingfei accepted the “grapes” and said softly, “Thank you.”
“Brother.” A voice seemed to sound behind him.
Lu Mingfei stiffened and spun around. There was nothing there. Only the lamplight trembled slightly.

“Two people, both boys… lived here,” Nono said softly. “One was taller than the other… so his robe was longer. They might have been brothers. The younger one was quiet and had trouble moving… The older one made things to help him.” Nono closed her eyes and thought for a long time. “They spent a lot of time in this room every day. The younger one wrote, while the older one sat across the table and watched him… The sunlight would have been lovely in spring, because the window faced the sun… In winter they would light a brazier and sit around it for warmth… The older brother loved the younger one very much, but he was strict too… It was lonely… At sunset, they would go a long time without speaking.”
Nono slowly opened her eyes. “This is Dragon King Norton’s bedchamber. I think it is.”
“You’re just guessing, aren’t you?”

“No. It’s profiling, a method commonly used in criminal psychology. You collect evidence, think about the criminal’s psychology, and reconstruct information about them. There’s a great deal of information left in this room: two robes of the same material and cut hanging on the wall, mechanisms that can be operated, a thick stack of paper, a low table… Put yourself in the owner’s place and think, and slowly you start to feel you understand what he was thinking. That’s profiling. I don’t know why, but I’m very good at it. No one taught me. When I was little, I could walk into a room, sit there for a few hours, and guess what kind of person lived there.” Nono said, “Do you remember when I first met you?”
Lu Mingfei blinked and nodded.
“Haven’t you always wondered why I helped you? I rarely meddle in other people’s business. Even Caesar says I’m a cold person.”
“Yeah, I have,” Lu Mingfei admitted.

“Because the first moment I saw you, you felt familiar. Before I came out, I stood a long way off and watched you crying for a long time. I could imagine what kind of person you were. You had an interview that day, but you hadn’t dressed properly or done much with your hair, which showed you didn’t care that much about it. There was dust on your backside, which showed you had a habit of sitting on the ground—by the roadside, perhaps… or on a rooftop?”
Lu Mingfei’s eyes widened. It had indeed been a rooftop. He had sat there for hours the night before the interview.

“You always kept your head down, so you must have been looking at a screen a lot.” Nono half closed her eyes. “You used a laptop… You liked someone, but she wasn’t your girlfriend. I could see it in your eyes. Then I knew what sort of person you were. Just as I can imagine the two people living in this room now: warm, gentle, but lonely too.”
“But you said the window faced the sun. How can you tell that?” Lu Mingfei found it incredible.
“This place smells of sunlight,” Nono said softly.
“Anyway, leaving the bomb here can’t be wrong, can it?” Lu Mingfei said. “We’re running low on oxygen. Wandering around blindly won’t help.”
“Mm!” Nono nodded. “Let’s do that! The Dragon King used to live here. It meant a lot to him. Maybe he even came back…”

“Hey! Don’t scare me! What do you mean, came back? If a dragon comes down from above in a minute, what do we do? Say, ‘Hello, have you eaten?’” Lu Mingfei hurried to stop that awful thought. “We’re here to wreck the place, so let’s get on with it!”
“Right. We’re here to wreck the place.”

Nono set the black box she carried on the low table and opened it. The thing inside looked like a nineteenth-century radio: red liquid bubbled slowly in a blown-glass tube, and wires of all colors were connected in a tangle. Lu Mingfei thought whoever had put the circuit together must certainly have failed Principles of Electrical Engineering.

“Don’t underestimate it. Equipment Department gear is usually reliable, although sometimes the power is a bit excessive. We can’t ask Professor Schneider right now. How about forty-five minutes?” Nono turned the brass dial on the device, and a little red bulb began to blink.
“Hey! Give people a little warning, will you? How can you just press it as soon as you say it?” Lu Mingfei jumped up and ran for the door.

“There’s enough time. The communications cable was cut, but it’s still outside. We only have to follow it out. Coming in took fifteen minutes, and with ten minutes to ascend, we’ll still have twenty minutes when we get back to the ship. Enough for a game of StarCraft.” Passing the table with the little lamp, she drew a diving knife from behind her waist. “Let’s cut it off and take it as a souvenir.”
“What kind of warped taste is that? Are you one of those inconsiderate tourists?” Lu Mingfei said.

“This place is about to disappear. The traces of the lives lived here, this room, all of it will disappear. Even the scent that lingers here will be gone. Thinking of it that way, I feel we ought to keep something to remember it by.” Nono grasped the bronze palace maid and suddenly froze.
The lamp lifted easily in her hand. It was not joined to the table beneath it as she had imagined.
“What is it?” Lu Mingfei asked.
Nono looked at him, her expression strange. “Use your brain…”
“My cerebrum or my cerebellum?” Lu Mingfei said. “I’ve been using my cerebellum all along, so I can run faster.”
“This is just an ordinary lamp…” Nono said.
“What’s wrong with an ordinary lamp?”
“Can an ordinary lamp burn for thousands of years? Who… filled it with oil?”
Lu Mingfei froze, his scalp prickling as though ten thousand little insects were crawling over it. He shuddered and looked sharply up at the waterwheel used as an elevator. It was still turning.
Who had filled it with oil? Surely it wasn’t a housekeeper paid by the hour. Or had the owner only just left?

Lu Mingfei and Nono jumped onto the bronze waterwheel. One side descended, the other ascended. Near the top, they saw a bronze plate bearing a face in relief: the living spirit that guarded the entrance. This time Lu Mingfei needed no prompting. He pulled off his diving glove and rubbed his hand over the living spirit’s lips.
When his life was at stake, he did not mind giving a little blood.

The bronze plate opened as though melting. At the same time, a tremendous suction carried them upward, and by the time they could see their surroundings, they were underwater again. In his haste to escape, Lu Mingfei had forgotten his mask. He swallowed a mouthful of the corpse-soaked water he found so disgusting and nearly choked. By the time he had fumbled his mask on and connected the oxygen, he saw Nono floating in the water, looking around. In the beam of her lamp, her face was pale.
“Hurry!” Lu Mingfei said.
“Which way?” Nono asked. “Haven’t you noticed? The communications cable… is gone!”

Lu Mingfei’s heart nearly stopped. Their communications cable had been cut at the entrance, so its end should still have been outside. But now it was gone, every bit of it. He and Nono could still talk because a short cable linked the two of them.
“The current here is slow. It shouldn’t have carried the cable away. Someone… took it,” Nono said.

“Don’t say frightening things like that. It sounds like a ghost story! It couldn’t be the Dragon King, could it? Would he bother? He could just breathe fire and burn us to death.” Lu Mingfei forced himself to sound brave.
“The water pressure is lower here,” Nono said.
Lu Mingfei looked at the pressure gauge. The pressure had fallen by half, meaning the water above them had suddenly become shallower.
“Something is happening,” Nono said.
“What could be happening?” Lu Mingfei pricked up his sensitive rabbit ears.

Then he heard it: a faint scraping, growing louder and louder until it became a thunderous rumble. Lu Mingfei could not say what the sound was. He felt like a tiny man inside a mechanical watch, listening to it run: countless metal gears meshing, bearings turning, the balance oscillating. Those tiny sounds had been magnified hundreds and thousands of times.
“The bronze city has started moving!” Nono said. “Someone activated it. The falling water level means water is draining out somewhere else, creating the power to drive the city.”

A huge circular shadow descended from above. Lu Mingfei watched it settle on the bottom not far away and sink into the pile of bones, crushing remains that had slept for thousands of years into powder. It was a bronze gear as large as a millstone, weighing perhaps several tons.
More bronze gears fell, churning the water. Then came large bronze fragments carved with patterns of branches and leaves. The ceiling had begun to collapse too.
“You’ve got to be kidding! Is this it running? It’s collapsing!” Lu Mingfei stared.
“Has its self-destruction been activated?” Nono took a deep breath. “Norton once destroyed his bronze palace in northern Europe himself, sinking it into the Ice Sea.”
“There’s no time to study this guy’s demolition history! Look up!” Lu Mingfei shouted.

Nono raised her head and saw a nightmare. Among the falling bronze fragments, a gigantic snake face emerged. The statue of Dragon King Norton had toppled. Eight stories high, the colossus sank amid violent undercurrents, falling straight toward their heads.
“Down below!” Without waiting for an answer, Nono pressed Lu Mingfei’s hand against the living spirit’s face on the bottom.

Swept along by the pouring current, they entered the Dragon King’s bedchamber again. A moment later a crack like an earthquake came from above. Presumably the bronze statue had reached the bottom. The whole room shook, ready to collapse at any moment.
“There’s another passage directly below!” Nono shouted. “That’s the route Ye Sheng and Aki took last time!”

The door guarded by the living spirit had cracked. Even walls made of material as supple as regenerated metal could not withstand an impact so violent. Water swept over the bronze waterwheel, carrying them downward. There they plunged straight down into another bottomless body of water. Before Lu Mingfei could look around, a violent torrent poured from the exit above onto his head.
“The level above is full of water!” Nono shouted. “It’ll flood level by level! Exactly what Ye Sheng and Aki ran into! Do you remember the route through the bronze-city map you solved last time?”
“No!” In his urgency, Lu Mingfei did not know how to explain. “Down. Just keep going down!”

“Let’s gamble on it!” Nono pulled out an emergency hemostatic bandage, wrapped it tightly around his wrist, and tied a firm knot. “Open your oxygen valve all the way, increase the pressure! We have plenty of oxygen, unlike Ye Sheng and Aki then. Your hand can be exposed, but don’t undo this knot. Once your oxygen leaks out, you won’t have another chance! Understand?”
“Understood!” Lu Mingfei nodded hard, shaking like a sieve.
“Dive now. I’ll cover you.” Nono looked into Lu Mingfei’s eyes, where a timid, frightened soul was trembling.

She reached out and stroked his head, then was silent for a moment. “Maybe I really shouldn’t have brought you down. I thought it would be easy… But being afraid doesn’t help. Remember when I walked up to the screening room? You stood there looking like some poor wretch, shoulders hunched and head down. I hate seeing people like that, because I used to hunch my shoulders and lower my head too, standing in a corner where no one looked at me… It doesn’t help. It won’t make you feel better.”
“Even at the hardest moment, you have to look as if you arrived in a Maybach!” Nono gave a faint smile. The beam of the lamp fell on her pale face.
“Could you not make it sound like goodbye forever?” Lu Mingfei said.
“Bullshit! I’m saying it so we won’t have to say goodbye forever! Dive!” Nono shouted.
The forward cabin of the Moniach was deathly quiet.

The monitor still showed the connection as broken. The Moniach had lost contact with the dive team, for reasons unknown. Manstein and Caesar had been staring at the screen for fifteen minutes, ever since the connection failed, without looking away.
Caesar’s mouth was set tight. Manstein breathed heavily.
“Fifteen minutes have passed. Their chances of survival are already low,” Manstein said quietly.

“We should send a second dive team now,” Caesar said coldly. “The second team can be me alone, or we can draw from the others! Their oxygen should last at least another hour and a half. As long as it hasn’t run out, they’re not dead! I’m completely ready to dive.”

“Do you know what my Yanling is?” Manstein looked into Caesar’s eyes. “Snake, the same as Ye Sheng’s. But my domain is larger than his; it reaches the bottom. There’s violent activity down there. You’ve felt it too, haven’t you? Water carries sound well. What has your Kamaitachi heard?”
“Noise. Terrible noise,” Caesar said.

“I can’t tell what’s happening down there, but the Dragon King may have been awakened. No one can dive now! I need everyone to stay at their posts. I came here to kill the Dragon King,” Manstein said. “I’ll wait for him right here. Caesar, you know what would happen if a dragon were let loose in the human world. Everything concerning dragons must be sealed inside a black box. That’s our mission!”
Caesar stared fiercely into Manstein’s eyes until a Student Council officer came up and laid a hand on his shoulder.
“Caesar, I can see fear in your eyes.” Manstein glanced at his watch. “If they’re alive, their oxygen can last another hour and a half. In one hour, you can go down to rescue them.”
Lu Mingfei and Nono struggled in the underwater current.

Millions of tons of water in the bronze city were pouring downward through different entrances. The force of the water drove the city’s machinery, but it seemed to be working toward its own destruction. The vast, intricate city was as though alive, and now it gave a dying wail.
Lu Mingfei clung desperately to Nono’s wrist. The only thing connecting his life to the world now was her hand.

Countless passages lay below, like a chemical plant of the industrial age. Strangely shaped valves opened and closed; pipes joined and broke apart, diverting the currents to entirely different places. Enormous waterwheels spun at high speed under the force. They had no choice but to enter the nearest passage. Only seconds later, a huge bronze door closed behind them, almost cutting them in half. At the same time, immense water pressure threatened to flatten them as the passage began to flood.
Nono swam fast, agile as a mackerel. All Lu Mingfei could do was kick his legs mechanically, contributing a little propulsion for her.

The pipes spread like a spiderweb, a maze full of water. They could not keep following the so-called route directly downward. In this constantly moving city, no path stayed fixed. For them, the route Ye Sheng and Aki had taken did not exist; going straight down had been a coincidence last time.
He was nearly exhausted. The hand exposed to the water had lost all feeling from the tight binding at the wrist and the cold. Lu Mingfei could not even tell whether it was still there.
It did not matter, though. They were about to die anyway.

They were completely lost. Lu Mingfei tried hard to recall the map of the bronze city. Every mechanism had been outlined on it, as if the person who drew it had watched the city being built. Remembering the map might help, but he also needed to understand how it worked. That was sheer nonsense!
Last time he had used nonsense to save Aki, but he could not use it again to save himself and Nono.

If the communications cable had not been cut, he could still have called Fingel, who was sitting at a computer ready to be excellent support. Now there was nothing to be done. Even if their backup were a god instead of Fingel, he would still need a connection to call on that god for help.
Maybe there was one last way. A light seemed to flash through Lu Mingfei’s mind. Some things could not be explained; at a time like this, he could only believe in those inexplicable things!
“Black Sheep Wall!” he shouted.
He did not know whether it would work. Strictly speaking, the cheat could only be entered after pressing Enter. The problem was that he did not even have a keyboard.
A burst of static sounded in his ear as irregular electrical current entered his headset.
“Lu Mingfei, Lu Mingfei, my dear useless junior, what are you doing? This is your useless senior Fingel’s two-hundred-and-fourteenth call. Please respond. Please respond…” Fingel’s lazy voice.
“Th-that works too?” Lu Mingfei was speechless.
“Damn it, hurry up! We’re dying underwater! Look up that map of the bronze city for me!” Lu Mingfei shouted as loudly as he could.
His voice boomed through the Moniach’s forward cabin at the same time. Everyone was stunned.
“This…” Caesar rushed from his position to the console.

Manstein pressed a hand hard to his forehead. In his mind, the Snakes were restless. From a scientific standpoint, Snake was a form of bioelectric current. Ye Sheng had once used it to link directly to the Moniach’s radio equipment. For Manstein, who also possessed Snake, these ethereal Snakes were his loyal subordinates, obeying only his commands.
But now the Snakes were out of control! They returned at high speed and entered his consciousness in an instant. Lu Mingfei’s voice echoed not only from the speakers but also inside his head.
He struggled to give the Snakes orders, but to no effect.
The Snakes were carrying the signal, and he was serving as a relay between Lu Mingfei and the Moniach. Some incredible command had been issued, forcibly commandeering the power of Manstein’s Yanling!
“This is… cheating, isn’t it?” he wanted to say.
The ability surpassed every known rule.
The information transmitted from Lu Mingfei appeared in full on the screen: a map of the bronze city!

“Fingel! Pull up the earlier map! Find where we are! We’re lost, lost in the Dragon King’s house!” Every shout rang like thunder inside Manstein’s head, shaking him until he slumped weakly in his chair.
“Wait, wait, wait! I have to… I have to print it!” Fingel rushed frantically about the computer-filled office of the campus news network, roaring into the microphone.
The paparazzi around him, who had been dozing as they waited to post news from China online promptly, all woke with a start.
“Print! Find the transparency sheets! Print them for me!” Fingel stamped about among the computers.
The paparazzi displayed the utmost speed and dedication of news professionals. Two printed transparencies were quickly handed to Fingel. He laid one over the other and held them up to the light.
“Fingel, how are you on this channel?” Caesar demanded. “You hacked into a secure channel. That’s against college rules!”
“Give it a rest, third-year! If I hadn’t hacked the channel, your girlfriend would be dying with my useless junior!” Fingel was forceful in a way quite unlike his usual self.
Caesar immediately shut up.

“Forget the rules! Find their position! Fingel, you got a perfect score in magic-powered mechanics. You can do it!” Professor Guderian’s voice came over the channel. In the library control room, the old man was stamping around just like Fingel, as though he had springs on his feet.
“Shut up! I’m looking, looking, looking!” Cold sweat covered Fingel’s forehead.
“Faster!” Caesar came back on the channel. “Professor Manstein is nearing his limit.”

“Roger!” Fingel gritted his teeth, his face fierce. “Listen, good-for-nothing! You’re in a circular passage about two meters across. You just passed a sluice gate, and before that there were lots of wheels. Right?”
“That’s right!”

“I’ve worked it out. By the principles of magic-powered mechanics, the bronze city is operating much as it did last time, except the direction has been reversed. You attended the introduction to alchemical chemistry. The sign of alchemy is the pentagram. In ancient times, when sorcerers performed a ‘summoning of fire,’ they drew the pentagram from the top toward the lower right. Drawing it in reverse, from the lower right upward, meant ‘banishment of fire.’ The bronze city is operating in the latter mode now: self-destruction.”
“Is this the time for a lecture?” Lu Mingfei wailed. “Senior, get a grip!”

“I’m explaining the principle so you’ll believe me! If the city keeps running, it’ll be completely destroyed. You need to get out quickly! Ahead and below, there’s a square shaft. It’ll contract and disappear within minutes. That’s your way! I’ll tell you the next step soon!” Fingel sat at the computer, working the keyboard. “I need Norma’s support… Damn it, I only have F-rank clearance!”
“Use mine,” Guderian said. “I have B-rank clearance. My password is…”
“No need! I’m accessing it with A-rank clearance!”
“You… you’re hacking our system, aren’t you?” Guderian said.

“At a critical moment, hacking or not, black or white… as long as it works!” Fingel pressed Enter. The screen changed rapidly: A-rank access granted, database opened, computing resources prioritized, bandwidth greatly increased. Special functions authorized only for A-rank users appeared in his F-rank menu, which normally allowed him little more than checking his grades and ordering food.
“Norma, I’m counting on you.” Fingel was breathing hard.
“I will suspend all other computations and give priority to calculating the bronze city’s movements, providing timely information,” Norma said mildly. “Trust me. I’m a good GPS.”
“Caesar, look outside!” someone suddenly cried.

Caesar looked up. Beyond the porthole was a vast expanse of white vapor. At some point visibility had fallen to the level of dense fog. The reservoir was like a pot on the boil, giving off ever thicker white steam, dense as milk.

“He’s here. Norton, King of Bronze and Fire. His intense heat warmed the river water and produced a great deal of vapor. We overlooked the thermometer. The water outside is almost fifty degrees Celsius, too hot even for a hot spring,” Zero said. “It looks deliberate. He’s come to hunt us.”
“Professor Manstein?” Caesar shook Manstein’s shoulder.

Manstein’s whole body was limp. Only his pupils flickered rapidly. Yanling: Snake was working at overclocked speed, and all his remaining consciousness went into maintaining communications. The person in charge of Operation Bronze had been incapacitated. Caesar looked around. Most of those left were students, the elite he had chosen from the Student Council.
“First Mate Grayson, do you agree to my taking over as captain?” Caesar asked.
“I agree,” Grayson said without hesitation.

“I’m taking over Captain Manstein’s duties. Grayson, take the helm. Gunayal, monitor sonar. Naoki Kumagai, ensure the engine room has fuel. Pacino, check the torpedo compartment. Prepare the Shkval torpedo for launch.” Caesar issued his orders rapidly. “Zero, you’re in charge of firing the torpedo.”
“Me?” Zero asked calmly.

“Leave that sort of thing to someone who has no sense of danger. We have only one chance.” Caesar looked around. “Everyone, don’t panic! We’ll see him on sonar, then fire the torpedo. It’s that simple!”
“You perked right up as soon as you learned your girlfriend was all right,” Zero said.

“That has nothing to do with it. I just like powerful opponents.” As he spoke, Caesar loaded cartridges one by one into the sniper rifle he had prepared. The bullets glinted a dangerous dark red. The Equipment Department had supplied ample alchemical ammunition; as they had said, the ship was now fully armed.
The hull jolted violently, and a muffled impact came from below. Caesar’s expression changed. The sound had come from the torpedo compartment.
“Torpedo compartment breached! The warhead is destroyed!” the first mate roared over the headset.

In the torpedo compartment, the first mate could not believe his eyes. A black, spear-like object had thrust upward from the bottom of the ship, piercing the steel hull, the torpedo compartment, and the Shkval torpedo’s warhead.
A moment later came another muffled impact.
“Number three watertight compartment flooding!” This time the chief engineer shouted. “Someone’s hurt!”
“It’s the Dragon King! He’s attacking the bottom of the ship from underwater!”
A third muffled impact followed, and the ship began to list.
“Number two watertight compartment flooding! Fuel line leaking!”
“Fire! The aft compartment is on fire! Put it out! Quickly!”
Zero and Caesar looked at each other. The Moniach had six watertight compartments in all. Two were flooding now; if two more leaked, the ship would lose buoyancy and sink.
“Start the engines and accelerate!” Caesar roared. “If we stay still, we’re a target!”
The Moniach’s engines thundered as the ship zigzagged in great sweeps through the white mist on the river. Behind it, a sharp wake raced in pursuit.
“Hard left!” Caesar ordered.
The first mate at the helm hauled the wheel to port, and the Moniach traced a great arc through the water.
“Full power! Hard right!” Caesar ordered again.

The first mate hauled the wheel to starboard, and the Moniach heeled over. It was a perfect turn, but at that instant another muffled impact came from below. Another watertight compartment was leaking.
“The engines are nearly overheating!” The chief engineer jumped about in the scorching lower compartment.
“Never mind! Full power!” Caesar roared.

He knew he could not delay, not even a second. No one else could see clearly, not even on sonar, but his Kamaitachi knew that the dangerous shadow underwater was chasing the Moniach at fifty knots. He did not know how long their evasive tactics could last. The enemy’s surprise attack had been so unexpected that even sonar had not detected the Dragon King approaching beneath the ship.
“How could sonar have missed him?” He suddenly realized something was wrong.
“Check the sonar!” he shouted to the second mate, Gunayal.
Gunayal started the sonar self-test. A dozen seconds later, his face turned pale. “We… we have no sonar! The diagnostic says the sonar transmitter has been removed!”
“How is that possible?” Third Mate Pacino stared. “We checked it before we sailed! Besides, who would remove the sonar?”
“I know,” Zero said quietly, pointing outside the porthole.

Everyone looked and froze. A naked man, iron-gray all over, was passing outside the porthole, looking ahead without expression—a ghostly sight. As he passed the forward cabin, he casually tossed something inside. Gunayal recognized it at once.
“The sonar transmitter!” It was their missing transmitter.
The iron-gray man began to run, light flowing over his body like flames. At the bow he executed a perfect dive into the water.
“That’s…” Caesar drew a deep breath. “Dragon King Norton!”
From the bow, they saw the bright figure swimming underwater in the river, growing farther and farther from the Moniach.
“Binoculars.” Caesar held out his hand.
Someone immediately put a pair in it. Caesar adjusted the focus and found the figure.
“What’s he doing?” Pacino asked.
“I don’t know, but I’ll know soon…” Caesar’s body gave a slight start as he spoke.

Through the binoculars, a vast creature was rising from the water. Black scales flared all over its body; it shook itself sharply and hissed at the sky. Without binoculars, everyone could see the dragon shape stretching over the water, like a totem carved into a rock face by ancient people.
The bright figure swam toward the great dragon. It bent its long, slender neck; he seized its iron mask, and it lifted him from the water. He described a graceful arc and landed astride its neck.
“You’ve worked hard, Samson, all these years.” He gently stroked the dragon’s iron mask, his voice warm. Samson, the dragon servitor, answered with a long, low hiss.
Then he looked toward the distant ship and smiled silently.
Caesar saw the smile through the binoculars. He knew the Dragon King was smiling for him to see, and for some reason it sent a chill through him.

The Dragon King slowly removed the servitor’s iron mask and raised both hands, scorching flames flowing over them. Suddenly he plunged his hands into the servitor’s skull. The dragon shuddered violently but held on. It gave a low, dying moan and slowly closed its golden eyes. Its folded wings opened and lay flat on the water, keeping it balanced.
“Are they… turning on each other?” Aboard the Moniach, everyone watched in terror.
The Dragon King’s burning hands were consuming the great dragon’s brain. The dragon endured the terrible pain without moving, and even after it was over its lifeless body remained in place.

The Dragon King stood and stepped into the servitor’s empty skull. He raised his arms to the sky. Intense light streamed from his body into the dragon’s, and a pillar of fire shot upward. Amid his hoarse roar, the dragon’s body trembled violently; its enormous eyes opened and closed, and a point of golden flame burned like a solitary lamp in the extinguished pupils.

The Dragon King’s roar swelled, and so did the golden fire, quickly lighting the enormous eyes. The dragon spread its wings again, and every scale opened with a piercing sound like metal scraping metal.
The great heart that had stopped began to beat like a war drum.
The dragon shape stretched and twisted again, as though about to rise into the sky.
After a thousand years of silence, Dragon King Norton once more stood above the world in the majesty of a king.
“They’ve… fused!” Caesar said quietly.
“What a sorrowful sacrifice.” Two kilometers away, on an island in the middle of the river, Mai Sakatoku lowered her binoculars. She wore a black combat suit.

She opened a large silver case and took out and assembled the black metal parts inside. Soon a pitch-black sniper rifle took shape. Mai opened a smaller silver case. Nestled in the padding was a cylindrical quartz-glass tube containing a dark red cartridge. Its bullet looked like a roughly polished crystal, with light flowing inside it like blood.
Mai carefully loaded the cartridge into the chamber, then placed a call. “Everything is proceeding according to plan. I’m ready.”
“Has Norton appeared?”
“Yes, but he didn’t hatch. He took over the body of his dragon servitor, Samson.”

“Direct fusion saves time, but it means sacrificing a powerful member of his kind. Those people at Cassell College really have a limited understanding of dragons. It looks as though they don’t know about fusion at all.”
“It makes me sick. Like a parasite.”

“Samson would be willing. A dragon servitor will do anything for their monarch, and revenge is one of the things they most want to do,” the woman said. “I’ll repeat the order: Lu Mingfei must survive. Whether Norton, King of Bronze and Fire, lives or dies doesn’t matter.”
“Understood.” Mai hung up and raised her binoculars toward the Moniach in the thick fog, smiling. “Third-year, you need to hold out a little longer. I’m expecting a lot from you!”
